newsitem.title: USA: California gets electric deregulation bill.
newsitem.headline: California gets electric deregulation bill.

text.p: California Gov. Pete Wilson on Monday signed far-reaching legislation to open the state's $21 billion electricity market to competition and slash consumer rates by 20 percent by the year 2002.

"We're doing more than signing a new law, we are shifting the balance of power in California," Wilson, a Republican, said at the bill signing ceremony in San Diego. "We've pulled the plug on another outdated monopoly and replaced it with the promise of a new era of competition."

The state Legislature approved the deregulation plan in late August. Lawmakers described the measure as "historic" and a "model" for the nation since dozens of other states are considering similar proposals.

The sweeping measure will restructure the electric industry in California, ending the utility monopoly on generation and opening the market to competition so that retail customers can choose among electric energy suppliers.

The bill has the support of the large utilities that would be affected most, Pacific Gas and Electric Co., Enova Corp.'s San Diego Gas and Electric, and Edison International's Southern California Edison.

Supporters said deregulation would stimulate the state's economy, save schools over $123 million by the year 2002, ensure a reliable source of power and provide safeguards against widespread power outages.
Critics said the plan was a bailout for utilities.
The legislation lays out a five year transition period during which the industry will be opened to competition.
Residential users and small commercial businesses are guaranteed a rate reduction of 10 percent starting January 1, 1998, followed by another 10 percent reduction by 2002.
Currently, California's electrical rates are 40 percent higher than the national average -- 50 percent higher than Texas, 65 percent higher than Nevada and 120 percent higher than Oregon.

To help the investor-owned utilities better compete as the generation market opens, the utilities will be compensated for certain "stranded" costs, such as nuclear power plants, that would not be economical in a competitive market.
The legislation authorises the California Infrastructure Bank to issue up to $10 billion in revenue bonds to help the utilities pay off their stranded costs.
By issuing the bonds through the state bank, the utilities will obtain more favourable interest rates on the debt. State taxpayers would have no obligation or financial exposure.
The bond financings will provide substantial savings to the utilities, which will be passed on to the customers.
